content: Thiamine, also known as vitamin B1 or aneurine hydrochloride, is a member of the B vitamin family. It is a colorless compound with the chemical formula C12H17N4OS. Thiamine is water-soluble but insoluble in alcohol, and it decomposes when exposed to heat. Its molecular structure includes a pyrimidine ring and a thiazole ring. Thiamine was first identified in 1910 by Umetaro Suzuki in Japan during his research on how rice bran cured beriberi. He initially named it aberic acid, later referred to as orizanin, but he did not determine its chemical composition or recognize it as an amine. In 1926, Jansen and Donath successfully crystallized thiamine and named it aneurin, referring to its antineuritic properties. Its chemical composition and synthesis were elucidated in 1935 by Robert R. Williams, who also coined the name thiamine. There are four naturally occurring thiamine phosphate derivatives: thiamine monophosphate (ThMP), thiamine diphosphate (ThDP) or thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP), thiamine triphosphate (ThTP), and the recently discovered adenosine thiamine triphosphate (AThTP). Thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP), also known as thiamine diphosphate (ThDP), functions as a coenzyme for several enzymes involved in the decarboxylation and subsequent conjugation of alpha-keto acids to Coenzyme A. In mammals, these enzymes include pyruvate dehydrogenase and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase (key enzymes in carbohydrate metabolism), branched-chain alpha-keto acid dehydrogenase, 2-hydroxyphytanoyl-CoA lyase, and transketolase (which operates in the pentose phosphate pathway to synthesize NADPH and pentose sugars such as deoxyribose and ribose). In other species, TPP is involved in enzymes like pyruvate decarboxylase in yeast and various bacterial enzymes. TPP is synthesized by the enzyme thiamine pyrophosphokinase, which requires free thiamine, magnesium, and adenosine triphosphate (ATP). Thiamine triphosphate (ThTP) was historically thought to be a neuroactive form of thiamine. However, recent findings indicate that ThTP is present in bacteria, fungi, plants, and animals, suggesting a broader cellular role. In Escherichia coli, ThTP appears to play a role in the cellular response to amino acid starvation. Adenosine thiamine triphosphate (AThTP), also known as thiaminylated adenosine triphosphate, was recently discovered in E. coli, where it accumulates during carbon starvation. In E. coli, AThTP can constitute up to 20% of the total thiamine content. It is also found in smaller amounts in yeast, the roots of higher plants, and animal tissues. Thiamine is essential for the metabolism of carbohydrates and fats to produce energy. It is critical for normal growth and development and supports the proper functioning of the heart, nervous system, and digestive system. Thiamine is water-soluble and cannot be stored in the body; however, once absorbed, it is concentrated in muscle tissue. Dietary sources of thiamine include green peas, spinach, liver, beef, pork, navy beans, nuts, pinto beans, bananas, soybeans, goji berries, whole grains, breads, yeast, the aleurone layer of unpolished rice, and legumes. A deficiency in thiamine can lead to severe health issues, including neurodegeneration, muscle wasting, and even death. Causes of thiamine deficiency include malnutrition, chronic alcoholism, and diets high in thiaminase-rich foods (e.g., raw freshwater fish, raw shellfish, ferns) or anti-thiamine factors (e.g., tea, coffee, betel nuts). Well-known syndromes associated with thiamine deficiency include Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome and beriberi, both of which are common in individuals with chronic alcoholism. Thiamine deficiency is also thought to be prevalent in individuals with diabetes and may contribute to some of the complications associated with the disease. Thiamine deficiency can be diagnosed by measuring the activity of transketolase in erythrocytes. Thiamine levels can also be assessed directly in whole blood by converting thiamine into a fluorescent thiochrome derivative. However, some studies suggest that these tests may not always reveal a deficiency in vitamin B1. Genetic disorders affecting thiamine transport are rare but significant. Thiamine-Responsive Megaloblastic Anemia (TRMA) with diabetes mellitus and sensorineural deafness is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in the SLC19A2 gene, which encodes a high-affinity thiamine transporter. TRMA patients do not exhibit systemic thiamine deficiency, suggesting redundancy in the thiamine transport system. This led to the discovery of a second high-affinity thiamine transporter, SLC19A3. Some studies suggest that high doses of thiamine (e.g., 50 mg daily) may enhance mental acuity, although this has not been conclusively proven. Thiamine has also been investigated as an insect repellent. Some studies suggest that taking 25–50 mg of thiamine three times daily can reduce mosquito bites. High thiamine intake produces a skin odor that is undetectable to humans but repels female mosquitoes. It takes over two weeks for this odor to fully saturate the skin. Despite anecdotal evidence supporting the effectiveness of thiamine-based repellents, no clinical trials have been conducted to confirm their efficacy. A 2002 pilot study administered thiamine tetrahydrofurfuryl disulfide (TTFD) rectally to ten children with autism spectrum disorder and observed beneficial clinical effects in eight of them. However, this study has not been replicated, and a 2006 review by the same author did not mention thiamine's potential effects on autism.
